files.lesson.md: --- order: 5 unit: powers node: [AC9M7N01 n3, AC9M7N01 n4] title: Between the squares summary: "43 is not a perfect square, but it sits between 36 and 49, so √43 is between 6 and 7. Closer to 49 or to 36? Square a decimal to find out: 6.6² ≈ 43.6." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } connection: square-patch # data/connections/maths.yml hook: "A square vegetable patch needs 29 m² of soil. No whole number squares to 43, but a builder still needs to know the side, to the nearest 10 cm." app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8265 url: http://127.0.0.1:8265/index.html readySelector: "#sl-s" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: square.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$6.6^2 = 43.56$: just over 43. $6^2 = 36$ and $7^2 = 49$, so $\\sqrt{43}$ is between 6 and 7, about 6.6." } explainClip: query: { code: "@square.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Between two squares" say: "Find the perfect squares either side." clip: - caption: { text: "6² = 36: too small for 43.", say: "Six squared is thirty-six: too small." } - wait: 800 - caption: { text: "7² = 49: too big. So √43 is between 6 and 7.", say: "Seven squared is forty-nine: too big. The root is between six and seven." } - wait: 1600 - caption: { text: "Try tenths: 6.6² = 43.56, very close.", say: "Try tenths. Six point six squared is very close." } - click: Make s bigger - click: Make s bigger - click: Make s bigger - click: Make s bigger - click: Make s bigger - click: Make s bigger - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "6.6 × 6.6" } - wait: 1400 --- Most numbers are not perfect squares, but they still have square roots. $\sqrt{29}$ is the side of a square with area 29: no whole number, but somewhere between two. The method: find the perfect squares either side. $25 < 29 < 36$, and $\sqrt{25} = 5$, $\sqrt{36} = 6$, so $\sqrt{29}$ is between 5 and 6. Then try decimals to get closer. ## Predict: where is √43? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to an interval for √43 shows whether they use the squares either side, or halve, or think of 43's digits." check: type: predict q: "$\\sqrt{43}$ is between which two whole numbers?" options: ["6 and 7", "21 and 22", "3 and 4", "40 and 50"] actual: "6 and 7. 6² = 36 and 7² = 49, and 43 is between them. 21 and 22 come from halving: 21 × 21 = 441." ``` Which perfect squares are near 43? ## Run: as close as you can ```step stage: run insight: "Stepping the side in tenths until the square is as close to the target as possible estimates a root to one decimal place, and shows it is between the whole numbers found first." try: { playground: board, starter: "square.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "The dashed square has area 43. Change the side (in tenths) to make your square as close to 43 as you can. Was your prediction right?", when: "s = 6.6", explain: "6.5² = 42.25 (0.75 under) and 6.6² = 43.56 (0.56 over), so 6.6 is closer: √43 ≈ 6.6." } ``` The board says how far your square is from 43, over or under. ## Investigate: the squares either side ```step stage: investigate insight: "Bounding a root by the perfect squares either side gives an interval with reasons; Noah's halving is the squaring-as-doubling mistake run backwards." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "$\\sqrt{70}$ is between 8 and which whole number?" answer: "9" feedback: - ["35", "That is half of 70. Which perfect square comes after 64?"] - ["7", "7² = 49, which is less than 64. √70 is more than 8."] explain: "8² = 64 and 9² = 81, and 70 is between them, so √70 is between 8 and 9." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#noah" text: "Noah estimates $\\sqrt{50}$. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: square-double explain: "Line 2: the square root is not half (25 × 25 = 625). 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, so √50 is just over 7." - check: type: reasoning q: "A square garden bed has area 90 m². Between which two whole numbers of metres is its side? Write each step with its reason." steps: - ["$9^2 = 81$ and $10^2 = 100$", "these are the perfect squares either side of 90"] - ["$81 < 90 < 100$, so $9 < \\sqrt{90} < 10$", "a bigger square has a bigger side"] picks: - step: 1 options: ["Find the perfect squares either side of 90", "Halve 90: 45", "Divide 90 by 10: 9"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "45 × 45 = 2025: far too big. A root is not a half.", "9 is close, but this is not a reason: 90 ÷ 10 finds a tenth, not a root."] explain: "81 < 90 < 100, so the side is between 9 m and 10 m (about 9.5 m: 9.5² = 90.25)." ``` ### Bound it, then get closer Here is the method for $\sqrt{43}$. ```worked 36 < 43 < 49 :: Find the perfect squares either side of 43. 6 < \sqrt{43} < 7 :: Take their roots: √43 is between 6 and 7. 6.5^2 = 42.25 \quad 6.6^2 = 43.56 :: Square some tenths. 6.5 is under and 6.6 is over. \sqrt{43} \approx 6.6 :: 43.56 is closer to 43 (0.56 over) than 42.25 (0.75 under). ``` Now try one: between which whole numbers is $\sqrt{70}$? ### Find the mistake Read Noah's working. Square his answer to check it. ### With reasons Your working can be short notes. Then choose the reason for the key step. ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a new target on the board, a bigger root, an area from a perimeter (backwards), then which numbers are perfect squares at all." try: { playground: board, starter: "square.yml#twenty", height: 560 } tasks: - starter: "square.yml#twenty" hint: ["4² = 16 and 5² = 25, so start between 4 and 5.", "Compare how far 4.4² and 4.5² are from 20."] check: { type: board, text: "The dashed square has area 20 m². Make your square as close to it as you can.", when: "s = 4.5", explain: "4.4² = 19.36 (0.64 under), 4.5² = 20.25 (0.25 over): √20 ≈ 4.5." } - check: type: question q: "$\\sqrt{200}$ is between which two whole numbers?" options: ["14 and 15", "100 and 101", "19 and 20", "10 and 20, and no closer"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is half of 200.", "19² = 361: too big.", "You can get closer: 14² = 196 and 15² = 225."] explain: "14² = 196 and 15² = 225, and 200 is between them." - check: type: answer q: "A square has perimeter 36 cm. What is its area, in cm²?" answer: "81" feedback: - ["324", "That is 18². Find one side first: 36 ÷ 4."] - ["9", "9 cm is the side. The area is side × side."] explain: "Side = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm. Area = 9² = 81 cm²." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: which of these is a perfect square?" options: ["400", "40", "4000", "200"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "6² = 36 and 7² = 49: 40 is between.", "63² = 3969 and 64² = 4096: 4000 is between.", "14² = 196 and 15² = 225."] explain: "20² = 400. A perfect square needs a whole-number root." ``` ### Twenty Each task changes one thing. ### A bigger root ### Backwards: from the perimeter ### Perfect or not ## Practise: roots between ```step stage: practise insight: "An estimate to one decimal place, an interval, and a two-step problem, mixed; halving is the planted slip; the review keeps squares fresh." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Estimate $\\sqrt{30}$ to one decimal place. (5² = 25 and 6² = 36.)" answer: 5.5 tolerance: 0.05 explain: "5.4² = 29.16 and 5.5² = 30.25: 30.25 is closer to 30, so √30 ≈ 5.5." - check: type: question q: "$\\sqrt{150}$ is between which two whole numbers?" options: ["12 and 13", "75 and 76", "11 and 12", "15 and 16"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is half of 150.", "11² = 121 and 12² = 144: both under 150.", "15² = 225: too big."] explain: "12² = 144 and 13² = 169." - check: type: answer q: "A square floor needs 64 square tiles, each 1 m by 1 m. How much skirting board goes round the edge, in metres?" answer: "32" feedback: - ["8", "8 m is one side. Skirting goes round all 4 sides."] - ["256", "That is 4 × 64. Find the side first: √64."] explain: "Side = √64 = 8 m. Perimeter = 4 × 8 = 32 m." - check: type: answer q: "Review: work out $12^2$." answer: "144" feedback: - ["24", "That is 12 × 2. Squaring is 12 × 12."] explain: "12 × 12 = 144." ``` ### To one decimal place ### Between ### Two steps ### Review: squares ## Make: an area in the thirties ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing a side whose square lands between 30 and 40 turns the bounding argument round: the side must be between √30 and √40." try: { playground: board, starter: "square.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["5² = 25 is too small and 6² = 36 is inside. Are there others?", "Step in tenths: 5.5² = 30.25."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a square whose area is between 30 and 40.", when: "a > 30 and a < 40", explain: "Any side from 5.5 to 6.3 works: √30 ≈ 5.48 and √40 ≈ 6.32." } ``` Then find the smallest and the biggest side (in tenths) that work. ## Make: a vegetable patch on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Bounding the side by the squares either side, then squaring tenths, is the whole method; the paper task makes them say why the side is between two whole numbers before they use it." hint: ["Which two perfect squares is 90 between?", "Try 9.4, 9.5 and 9.6 squared, and see which is closest to 90."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A community garden has a square vegetable patch with an area of 90 m². Edging is bought by the metre and goes right round the patch. How much edging is needed, to the nearest metre?" steps: - ["The side is $\\sqrt{90}$", "the side of a square is the number that squares to its area"] - ["$9^2 = 81$ and $10^2 = 100$, so the side is between 9 and 10", "90 is between 81 and 100"] - ["$9.5^2 = 90.25$ is the closest tenth, so the side is about $9.5$ m", "90.25 is only 0.25 over; 9.4² = 88.36 is 1.64 under"] - ["Edging $= 4 \\times 9.5 = 38$ m", "a square has 4 equal sides, so the edging goes round all four"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why is the side between 9 and 10?" options: - "90 is between 9² = 81 and 10² = 100" - "90 is between 9 and 10 tens" - "Half of 90 is 45, which is near 9 × 5" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Compare 90 with the squares of the whole numbers, not with 9 and 10 themselves.", "Halving is not the way back from squaring: 45 × 45 is far too big."] answer: "38" feedback: - ["9.5", "That is one side. The edging goes round all four."] - ["360", "That is 4 × 90. Find the side first: it is the square root of 90."] criteria: - "I found the side from the area, not the area times 4." - "I said which two squares 90 is between." - "I squared a tenth or two to get as close to 90 as I could." - "I multiplied the side by 4 for the edging." explain: "The side is √90, between 9 and 10 because 81 < 90 < 100. 9.5² = 90.25, so the side is about 9.5 m. Edging goes round 4 sides: 4 × 9.5 = 38 m. (The corners overlap a little, so a gardener buys a bit extra.)" ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The area is made up for the task, but the question is real: edging, fencing and turf for a square plot all start from its side. Show the two squares either side, then your tenths, and type the length of edging. **Also used in** - **Building.** Square paving, rooms and tiles of a known area: the side comes from the square root, and skirting or edging from the perimeter. - **Checking an answer.** The squares either side catch a wrong key press: a calculator saying √90 = 45 is clearly off. - **Pythagoras.** The longest side of a right-angled triangle is a square root, and "between 9 and 10" is the first check on it. ```teacher summary: Students bound a square root between two whole numbers using the perfect squares either side, estimate it to one decimal place by squaring tenths on a grid board, and solve area and perimeter problems with roots (AC9M7N01, nodes 3 and 4). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can say which two whole numbers a square root is between, with a reason. - I can estimate a square root to one decimal place by squaring decimals. - I can solve problems with the side, area and perimeter of a square. struggle: Choosing between two neighbouring decimals (6.5 or 6.6). Ask which square is closer to the target and by how much, and let them compare the two distances. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need the perfect squares to 144 (previous lesson) and multiplying decimals (calculators are fine for squaring tenths). The one idea: find the perfect squares either side, take their roots, and the answer lies between. The scaffold matters: without it students guess, or halve (Noah's mistake). The reasoning check never marks the free working; only the reason for the key step is chosen and marked. running: - "Predict: students who chose 21 and 22 halved. Ask them to square 21." - "Run: ask whether 6.6 is a little over or under, and how they decided between 6.5 and 6.6." - "Investigate: chant the routine: squares either side, roots, between." - "Modify: in the perimeter task, ask which is known first: the side or the area?" - "Make: collect sides that work and order them; the ends approach √30 and √40." - "Paper: the vegetable patch is worked in books; the page marks the answer (38 m) and the reason the side is between 9 and 10. Books out, then look for the two squares either side written before any decimal." stuck: - see: A student halves the number (Noah's mistake). ask: Square your answer. Do you get the number back? fix: The root times itself gives the number; use the squares either side. - see: A student finds the interval but cannot get closer. ask: Square 6.5. Is it over or under 43? fix: Square tenths and compare the distances. - see: A student mixes up side and area in a problem. ask: Is this number a length or an area? fix: Root for area to side; square for side to area. stretch: Between which two whole numbers is √1000? Estimate it to one decimal place, then check with a calculator. support: Keep the list of squares to 144 visible and use a number line marked with 36, 43 and 49. leads: > Next: exponent notation, prime factors and HCF and LCM (AC9M7N02). Where it leads: Pythagoras (Year 8) gives lengths like √20, and estimating them first checks a calculator answer. exit: q: Between which two whole numbers is √55? Give a reason. a: 7 and 8, because 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, and 55 is between them. explain: > For a number that is not a perfect square, find the **perfect squares either side**: $36 < 43 < 49$. Their roots give the whole numbers either side: $6 < \sqrt{43} < 7$. To get closer, square decimals: $6.5^2 = 42.25$ and $6.6^2 = 43.56$. The closer one wins: $\sqrt{43} \approx 6.6$. (A square root is not a half: $\sqrt{50}$ is about 7, not 25.) ```
